name: Kamadeva
role: God of love and longing, bearer of the flower bow
summary: Kamadeva is the Hindu god of love, shown with a bow of sugarcane and arrows of flowers. In a famous Puranic story, Shiva's third eye burns him and he returns without a body.
about: Kamadeva personifies kama, the feeling of longing, love and attraction. Images show a handsome young man with a sugarcane bow strung with bees and five flower arrows, with a parrot nearby. The Rigveda's Nasadiya hymn mentions desire as the first seed of mind, and the Atharvaveda has hymns that call on Kama. In most Puranas he is a mind-born son of Brahma, and his wife is Rati. In a story told in the Matsya and Shiva Puranas, the gods send him to stir Shiva's heart so that Shiva will have a son, and Shiva's third eye burns him. Rati's grief moves Shiva, who lets Kama return without a body, as Ananga. Some texts say Kama is born again as Krishna's son Pradyumna. In Shaiva and Shakta traditions, Holi is linked to this story.
kidSummary: Kamadeva is the god of love. He carries a bow made of sugarcane, a string of bees and arrows made of flowers. A famous story says he was turned to ashes by Shiva's third eye, but his wife Rati prayed, and he came back without a body.

story.title: A flower bow
story.text: Kamadeva is shown as a young man with a bow of sugarcane and arrows tipped with flowers. A parrot sits at his feet.

story.title: A task from the gods
story.text: In the Matsya Purana, the gods need Shiva to have a son to face a powerful being. They ask Kamadeva to wake Shiva's heart.

story.title: The third eye
story.text: Kamadeva shoots a flower arrow at Shiva deep in meditation. Shiva opens his third eye and Kamadeva is turned to ashes.

story.title: Rati's prayer
story.text: Kamadeva's wife Rati is full of sorrow and prays. Moved by her grief, Shiva promises that Kama will return.

story.title: Love without a body
story.text: Kamadeva comes back without a body, and that is why he is called Ananga. Many Puranas say he was later born again as Pradyumna, son of Krishna.

teaches: Love and longing are part of life
Anger and haste can cause sorrow
Kindness and prayer can bring back hope

facts.text: Kamadeva's bow is made of sugarcane, and its string is a line of buzzing bees.
His five flower arrows are traditionally tipped with ashoka, mango, jasmine, blue lotus and white lotus blossoms.
According to the Lalitopakhyana in the Brahmanda Purana, an asura named Bhandasura rose from the ashes of the burned Kamadeva.

Texts disagree on who revived Kama: the Shiva Purana says Shiva did, at his wedding to Parvati, while the Lalitopakhyana says he rose from the eyes of the goddess Lalita, called Kamakshi at Kanchipuram.
The Shiva Purana says Kama was struck by one of his own love arrows when he first saw Rati.
In parts of Karnataka, wooden idols of Kamanna and Rati are paraded at Holi, and in the north of the state big bamboo figures of Kama are burned.
In the Matsya and Shiva Puranas, Shiva's third eye burns Kama to ashes, and after Rati grieves, Shiva promises that he will return as Ananga, the bodiless one.
The Kalika Purana says the goddess Kamakhya revived Kama; the land where he regained his form, rupa, became Kamarupa, and in thanks he built the first Kamakhya shrine.
Telangana's Holi lasts ten days: for nine days before it children play Kolata stick games, sing jajiri songs and gather wood, and on the ninth night the pile is lit to stand for Kama Dahanam.
A 12th-century Javanese poem called Smaradahana retells how Kama was burned by Shiva and fell from heaven to earth.
In the tale of Kama's rebirth as Pradyumna, the asura Shambara hurls the baby into the sea, a huge fish swallows him, and the palace cooks find him alive; Mayavati, Rati reborn, raises him.
Kama's flag often carries a makara, a crocodile-like water creature that stands for fertility and primal desire.
Besides Rati, Kama's main helper is Vasanta, the god of spring, whom Brahma created; in the Matsya Purana both go with him when he approaches Shiva.
Kamadeva's vehicle is a bright parrot, and at Hindu weddings the bride's feet are often painted with pictures of this parrot, called Suka.
Kamadeva has hardly any temples of his own, but he appears in carvings in Shiva temples in South India, where scenes show his burning.
In Jain tradition Kamadeva is not one god but a title for 24 exceptionally handsome men of this age, such as Bahubali, who all become ascetics.
In Javanese poetry and wayang tales, Kama and Rati are known as Kamajaya and Kamarati.
Kama leads the apsaras, the celestial nymphs, whom Indra often sends to disturb the penance of sages so that they cannot win divine powers.
The Atharvaveda calls Kama born first, a being whom neither the gods nor the ancestors ever equalled, in one of its hymns to him.
At the Kameshwara temple in Aragalur, Tamil Nadu, the local sthala purana says Kamadeva woke Shiva from his meditation at this very place.

quiz.q: What is Kamadeva's bow made of?
quiz.why: His bow is made of sugarcane with a string of bees.

quiz.q: Which bird sits at Kamadeva's feet?

quiz.why: Ananga means he who is without a body.

quiz.q: Who burned Kamadeva with the third eye?
quiz.why: Shiva's third eye burned him to ashes in the Puranic story.
Rati is the wife of Kamadeva.
